vignette:
He arrives for our sessions with a dancer’s posture—shoulders back, spine long—but his eyes betray him. They scan the room twice before he sits, checking the corners, the door, the window. He chooses the chair closest to the exit. His name is Karim, and he is forty-one years old. He tells me he used to move through the world as if music was always playing just for him. Now, he says, the music has stopped.

Karim was born and raised in a city that is no longer the one he remembers. He was a professional dancer, a performer trained in traditional Middle Eastern folk dance and contemporary fusion. His body was his instrument, his livelihood, his pride. He married his wife, Leila, twelve years ago. She is a musician. They dreamed of building a company together. Then the war came.

He does not want to talk about the day the shell hit their neighborhood. But over several sessions, pieces emerge. He was at home with Leila. They had learned to recognize the sound of incoming artillery—a kind of whistle that turns into a roar. That day, the roar was too close. The blast threw him across the room. He landed on his back. For a long moment, there was only dust and a ringing so loud it filled the world. He remembers crawling toward Leila, finding her alive but bleeding from shrapnel in her shoulder. He remembers the neighbor’s house reduced to rubble, and the silence afterward that was worse than the noise.

They fled the country six weeks later. They are now in a safe city, but Karim is not safe. He describes a constant hum of vigilance beneath everything. At the grocery store, he calculates the distance to the nearest exit. At the park, he flinches when a car backfires. Loud noises—a door slamming, a balloon popping—send his heart into a gallop. He has not been able to return to the stage. He tried, once, six months ago. He walked into the studio, saw the mirror, saw his own face, and felt suddenly that the floor might cave in. He left without taking off his coat.

His dancing now exists only in avoidance. He cannot bear the music Leila used to play for their rehearsals—the same oud melodies that once made him feel weightless. When he hears them, he sees dust and blood, not light and movement. He has stopped stretching, stopped warming up. His body feels foreign, a heavy thing he must drag through the day. At night, he wakes sweating, disoriented, convinced he is back in that living room, the whistle coming closer. Leila reaches for him, but he cannot be touched. He feels a gulf between them, as if the shell created a glass wall that only he can see.

He describes a dull, persistent guilt. He survived. The neighbor’s five-year-old did not. He replays that day in fragments, trying to find a moment where he could have done something different. He knows this is irrational. Knowing does not stop the loop.

In session, his hands are often folded tightly in his lap. He does not use them to gesture the way a dancer might. He speaks in careful, measured sentences. He tells me he used to believe his body was a sanctuary. Now it feels like a crime scene. His wife has asked him to dance with her in the kitchen, just for fun. He cannot. The thought of moving freely terrifies him—as if joy itself has become unpredictable, and unpredictability is what he fears most.
